concepts.title: Tokens, Tokenization, and Context Windows
concepts.description: Every LLM operates over tokens, not words or characters, and the context window's fixed token budget, shared between everything you send in and everything the model writes back, is one of the most consequential constraints on what you can build with it.
learningObjectives: Explain why LLMs operate on subword tokens rather than characters or whole words, and what problem that design solves.
Describe roughly how byte-pair-style tokenization splits text, and predict which kinds of text will tokenize efficiently versus poorly.
Explain what a context window is, what counts against it, and what happens when a request exceeds it.
Identify the practical consequences of a finite context window: per-token cost, latency, and the 'lost in the middle' attention effect.
Choose an appropriate strategy -- truncation, chunking, summarization, or retrieval -- when input doesn't fit in the available budget.

sections.heading: Why Tokens, Not Characters or Words
sections.body:
Every LLM you'll integrate with, whether through an API or a local weights file, consumes and produces sequences of **tokens**, not characters and not whole words. That's an engineering compromise, and knowing why it was chosen tells you a lot about how the model behaves.

If a model operated on individual characters, sequences would become very long very fast (an average English sentence is roughly 5x more characters than words), which matters because the computational cost of the attention mechanism inside a transformer grows faster than linearly with sequence length (doubling the length more than doubles the compute). Character-level models also have to learn spelling and morphology from scratch, spending model capacity on something a slightly larger unit would give for free.

If a model operated on whole words instead, you'd hit the opposite problem: an open vocabulary. Human language mints new words constantly (product names, typos, code identifiers, usernames, words in dozens of languages), and a fixed word-level vocabulary either explodes to millions of entries or has to map every unfamiliar word to a generic 'unknown' placeholder, throwing away information the model badly needs.

Subword tokenization is the compromise that avoids both failure modes: common whole words become single tokens (fast, cheap, and the model has seen them a billion times), while rare or novel words get decomposed into smaller, recurring subword pieces the model has also seen many times, just recombined differently. No token is ever truly 'unknown' -- worst case, an unfamiliar string gets broken all the way down to individual bytes, so the model can still represent any input; it just costs more tokens.

sections.heading: How Byte-Pair Tokenization Splits Text
sections.body:
The dominant family of tokenizers used in production LLMs is built on **byte-pair encoding (BPE)** or close variants of it. The vocabulary isn't hand-designed; it's learned from a large text corpus, offline, before the model itself is ever trained: start with every individual byte as its own token, then repeatedly find the most frequently-occurring adjacent pair of tokens in the corpus and merge that pair into a single new token, added to the vocabulary. Repeat that merge step tens of thousands of times and you end up with a vocabulary, typically 50,000 to 200,000 entries depending on the model family, that contains everything from single characters up through entire common words and even common short phrases.

In practice the patterns look like this: common English words ('the', 'is', 'running') are usually a single token. Less common words, technical jargon, and words in morphologically rich languages often split into two or three tokens ('tokenization' might become something like 'token' + 'ization'). Whitespace, punctuation, and capitalization typically affect where boundaries fall -- ' Hello' (with a leading space) and 'Hello' (without one) are frequently two different tokens, not the same token with a flag. Numbers and random-looking strings (UUIDs, hashes, hex-encoded data) tokenize especially poorly, often close to one token per character or per few characters, because the merge process never saw enough repetition in those strings to justify building bigger merged tokens for them.

The consequence for anyone building on these models: a block of JSON with long random IDs, or a paragraph in a language underrepresented in the training corpus, can consume several times more tokens than an equal-length paragraph of plain English, which hits both cost and context budget. Token counts also differ between model families, because each has its own tokenizer and vocabulary, so a count from one tokenizer is only an estimate for another model. Use the tokenizer or token-counting endpoint that matches the model you call.

sections.heading: The Context Window: One Shared, Fixed Budget
sections.body:
The **context window** is the maximum number of tokens a model can attend to in a single call -- and critically, it is one shared pool, not separate pools for input and output. Your system prompt, conversation history, any documents you paste or retrieve, the user's actual question, and the model's own generated response all draw from the same token budget. A model with, say, a 128,000-token context window doesn't give you 128,000 tokens of input *plus* however much output you want -- if your input consumes 127,900 tokens, you have roughly 100 tokens left for the entire response, no matter how large the window nominally is.

When a request's token count -- input alone, or input plus the requested maximum output length -- exceeds what the model supports, you don't get a degraded or partial response; you typically get an API error (something like a context-length-exceeded error) or, in some client libraries, silent truncation of the oldest content, which is arguably worse because nothing tells you it happened. Either way it's a hard wall, and it shows up as a production incident the first time a user pastes in something unusually long. Most APIs also count the output limit you request (max tokens) against the window up front, which is why the error in the chat-loop example below reports a 'completion' figure alongside the message tokens. Setting max tokens far higher than you need can therefore cause a context error on an input that would otherwise have fit.

A large context window means the model *can* attend to that many tokens. It says nothing about whether the model will use every part of that window equally well, which is the subject of the next section.

sections.heading: Practical Consequences: Cost, Latency, and Lost-in-the-Middle
sections.body:
Three practical effects follow from everything being measured, and paid for, in tokens. First, **cost scales with tokens**, typically at different per-token rates for input versus output -- a feature that processes long documents will cost noticeably more per call than one that processes short chat turns, and this is usually the biggest lever for controlling LLM spend at scale, well before you start optimizing prompts for quality. Second, **latency scales with total tokens processed** -- both how much you send and how much you ask the model to generate -- so a chatty system prompt repeated on every single call, or an unnecessarily long requested output, measurably affects how snappy your feature feels.

Third, and less obvious: models do not attend to every position in a long context with equal effectiveness. Empirically and in practice, models tend to make best use of information near the very start and the very end of the context, with a measurable dip in retrieval accuracy for facts placed deep in the middle of a long input, an effect commonly called **'lost in the middle.'** So cramming more relevant material into the window is not a free win even when it fits the token budget; a shorter, well-curated context that puts the most important information near the edges of the prompt can outperform a longer one that buries it in the center.

Context window size is a budget to spend deliberately, not a resource to maximize: aim for the smallest context that reliably contains what's needed, not as much as will fit.

sections.heading: Strategies When Your Input Doesn't Fit
sections.body: When the material you want the model to see is larger than the available budget, you have a few options, each with different tradeoffs. **Truncation**, cutting off content past some length, is the cheapest to implement and the riskiest: you're gambling that whatever gets cut wasn't important, with no principled way to know. **Chunking and processing separately** (sometimes called a map-reduce pattern) splits the input into pieces that each fit comfortably, processes each piece independently (say, summarizing each chunk of a long document), then combines those intermediate results, possibly with another pass over the combined summaries -- this scales to very large inputs but costs more total tokens and more calls, and can lose cross-chunk context that spans a boundary. **Summarization as compression** shrinks earlier content (like older turns of a long conversation) into a denser summary before it's fed forward again, trading some fidelity for a smaller footprint. And **retrieval** -- covered in full in the next module -- sidesteps the problem: instead of trying to fit everything, you select only the material relevant to the current request and feed in just that. In production systems, retrieval is usually the default answer to 'my knowledge base is bigger than the context window,' while chunking or summarization is usually the answer to 'this one input is bigger than the context window.'

examples.title: Counting Tokens Before You Call the API
examples.code:
import tiktoken

encoding = tiktoken.get_encoding("cl100k_base")

english = "The quarterly report is due on Friday."
random_ids = "a3f9c2-8b1e-4d7a-91c0-f2e6b7d1a9c4"

print(len(encoding.encode(english)))      # around 8 tokens
print(len(encoding.encode(random_ids)))   # around 20+ tokens, despite being a similar length string
examples.explanation: Both strings are a similar character length, but they tokenize very differently, because of repetition in the corpus the tokenizer was built from. 'The quarterly report is due on Friday.' is made of common English words that appeared constantly during BPE merge-learning, so each maps to one token. The UUID-like string almost never appeared as repeated substrings during that process (nothing would have pushed a merge step to combine 'a3f' into one token), so the tokenizer falls back to much smaller pieces, close to a token every couple of characters. The counts in the comments are approximate; run the code to see yours. This is why logs, IDs, hashes, and other structured-but-unnatural text blow through token budgets and cost far more than their character count suggests. Check with the tokenizer for your model before you ship instead of estimating by character or word count.

examples.title: Watching Rare Words Split Into Subword Pieces
examples.code:
import tiktoken

encoding = tiktoken.get_encoding("cl100k_base")

for word in ["the", "tokenization", "antidisestablishmentarianism"]:
    token_ids = encoding.encode(word)
    pieces = [encoding.decode([t]) for t in token_ids]
    print(word, "->", pieces)

# 'the' -> ['the']                                   (1 token: extremely common)
# 'tokenization' -> ['token', 'ization']              (2 tokens: common word + common suffix)
# 'antidisestablishmentarianism' -> multiple fragments (5+ tokens: rare, decomposed further)
examples.explanation: The split points depend on the tokenizer and vocabulary a given model family uses, so treat the splits in the comments as representative of the pattern, not guaranteed output for every tokenizer. The pattern itself holds across BPE-family tokenizers. Extremely common words survive as a single token because the merge process saw enough repeated evidence to build one. A moderately common word built from a common root plus a common suffix splits into those pieces: 'token' and 'ization' each appeared often enough elsewhere to earn their own token, but 'tokenization' as a whole didn't earn a merge of its own. A rare word gets chopped into several fragments that may not look like meaningful sub-words to a human reader, since the tokenizer has no notion of morphology, only of statistical frequency in its training corpus. That's why domain-specific or jargon-heavy text (legal, medical, a codebase full of unusual identifier names) tends to consume noticeably more tokens per word than everyday prose.

examples.title: Hitting the Context Window Limit in a Chat Loop
examples.code:
conversation = [{"role": "system", "content": "You are a helpful assistant."}]

def send_turn(user_text, call_model):
    conversation.append({"role": "user", "content": user_text})
    reply = call_model(conversation)   # sends the ENTIRE history every single time
    conversation.append({"role": "assistant", "content": reply})
    return reply

# After enough turns, this raises something like:
# BadRequestError: This model's maximum context length is 128000 tokens.
# You requested 131204 tokens (128900 in the messages, 2304 in the completion).
examples.explanation: This is a common bug in chatbot code. The entire conversation history is resent on every turn (necessary, since the model has no memory between calls, so anything it should 'remember' has to be re-sent), so the token count of each request grows with every turn and nothing in the code bounds it. Nothing fails for a while, which is what makes it dangerous: it works in every quick manual test, then fails in production during the long, engaged conversations you'd most want to handle well. The error message itself is worth reading closely: it reports tokens used by the messages separately from tokens reserved for the completion, which shows that input and output share one combined budget. (The message above is illustrative; wording and numbers vary by provider.) You can't fix this by raising the limit, because you don't control the model's window. Manage the history instead: drop or summarize the oldest turns once the running total approaches a threshold below the maximum, leaving headroom for the response.

misconceptions.description: A token is roughly the same thing as a word, so you can estimate token counts by counting words.
misconceptions.clarification: For everyday English prose, a rough rule of thumb of about 4 characters or three-quarters of a word per token is a reasonable estimate -- but 'roughly the same as a word' breaks down for the content that matters most in production: numbers, IDs, code, punctuation-heavy text, and non-English languages routinely tokenize at a much worse (higher tokens-per-character) ratio than plain English prose. A word count will underestimate token usage for the inputs most likely to be long or unusual, so run the tokenizer for the model you're using.

misconceptions.description: A bigger context window means you should feed the model as much information as will technically fit, since more context can only help.
misconceptions.clarification: More context is not free and is not uniformly useful. It costs money and latency in proportion to the extra tokens, and models attend less reliably to information placed in the middle of a long context than to information near the start or end ('lost in the middle') -- so padding a prompt with marginally relevant material can degrade a response even when everything relevant is present somewhere in the window. The better default is to include only what's needed, positioned with care.

exercises.prompt: Two strings are roughly the same character length: a plain English sentence, and a string of randomly generated hexadecimal characters (like a hash). Both are passed through the same BPE-style tokenizer. Which one will produce more tokens, and roughly why?
exercises.code:
import tiktoken

encoding = tiktoken.get_encoding("cl100k_base")

sentence = "Please review the attached document before Monday."
hex_string = "9f8a3c1e7b2d4f6a0c9e8b7d3f1a5c2e"

print(len(encoding.encode(sentence)))
print(len(encoding.encode(hex_string)))
hints: Tokenizer vocabularies are built by repeatedly merging the most FREQUENT adjacent pairs seen in a large training corpus, not by any understanding of grammar or meaning.

Ask yourself: which of these two strings is more likely to contain substrings that recur constantly across a huge text corpus, and which is closer to random noise that never repeats in a learnable way?

Common English words and word-fragments earned single tokens because they appeared over and over during merge-learning. A random hex string, by construction, almost never repeats the same substring twice.
exercises.expectedAnswer: The hex string produces noticeably more tokens per character than the English sentence, even though both strings are a similar length. The sentence prints a small number of tokens (roughly 8-9), while the hex string prints a larger number (often close to one token per 2-3 characters; run it to see the exact count).
exercises.solutionExplanation: The English sentence is built from common words that have dedicated single tokens, because those words appeared very often in whatever corpus was used to learn the BPE merges. The hex string is effectively random from the tokenizer's point of view: nothing would have made a sequence like '9f8a' appear often enough elsewhere in the training corpus to justify merging it into its own token. The tokenizer falls back to much smaller units, producing more tokens for the same number of characters. BPE is driven by frequency, not meaning.

exercises.prompt: This chatbot function works fine in early testing but starts failing with a context-length error partway through long conversations. Find the underlying design bug and fix it so long conversations degrade gracefully instead of crashing.
exercises.code:
conversation = [{"role": "system", "content": "You are a helpful assistant."}]

def send_turn(user_text, call_model):
    conversation.append({"role": "user", "content": user_text})
    reply = call_model(conversation)
    conversation.append({"role": "assistant", "content": reply})
    return reply
hints: The entire `conversation` list is resent on every call, and it only ever grows: nothing removes or shrinks earlier turns.
Since input and output tokens share one fixed budget per call, a history that grows without bound will eventually leave no room for even a short reply.
You need a policy for what to do once the running conversation gets close to the model's limit -- consider dropping or summarizing the oldest turns while always keeping the system message.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The bug is a design flaw, not a syntax error: the code assumes conversation history can grow forever within a fixed-size budget. The fix adds a token-budget check (`count_tokens`) and a trimming policy (`trim_history`) that runs before every call, removing the oldest non-system turns once the running total passes a threshold safely below the model's maximum. Keeping the system message at index 0 and trimming from index 1 onward preserves the assistant's core instructions while older turns are discarded. A more sophisticated version would summarize the dropped turns into a short recap instead of deleting them, but trimming already turns a hard crash into bounded degradation. Note that `count_tokens` counts only message content; real chat formats add a few tokens of overhead per message, which the headroom below the limit absorbs.

assessments.prompt: A context window is described as '128,000 tokens.' What does that number actually limit?
options: The combined total of input tokens and output tokens for that single request.
Only the model's response length; you can send as much input as you want.
Only the text you send as input; the model's response doesn't count against it.
The number of separate messages you can include in a conversation, regardless of their length.
assessments.explanation: The context window is one shared budget covering everything in a single call: system prompt, conversation history, any retrieved or pasted content, the user's message, and the tokens the model generates in response. The “Only the text you send as input…” and “Only the model's response length; you can…” options each wrongly assume input and output have independent limits; consuming more on one side leaves less room on the other. The “The number of separate messages you can…” option is wrong because the limit is about total token count, not message count: one very long message can exceed the window on its own, and so can many short ones once their tokens add up.

assessments.prompt: A teammate proposes building a document Q&A feature by concatenating the full text of up to 200 uploaded PDFs into a single prompt, reasoning that the model's context window is 'large enough' since the combined text fits under the token limit. Explain why this is likely to perform poorly even if it technically fits, and what you'd propose instead.
assessments.modelAnswer: Fitting under the token limit is necessary for this to work at all, but far from sufficient for it to work well. Three problems stack up. First, cost and latency scale with total tokens processed, and 200 full PDFs concatenated together is very likely tens or hundreds of thousands of tokens -- every question the user asks would reprocess that entire mass of text from scratch, making the feature slow and expensive per query even if only a handful of sentences across those 200 documents contain the answer. Second, models don't attend to a long context uniformly -- the 'lost in the middle' effect means information buried deep within a huge concatenated blob is measurably less likely to be used correctly than information near the start or end, so relevant content from, say, document 140 out of 200 might be effectively ignored even though it's in the prompt. Third, this approach doesn't scale: the moment a 201st document is uploaded, or the total text creeps past the context window, it breaks outright. The better architecture is retrieval-augmented generation: index the documents ahead of time (chunk them and embed each chunk), and for each user question, retrieve only the small number of chunks that are actually relevant to that specific question, then include just those in the prompt. This keeps each call small, fast, and cheap regardless of corpus size, and it reduces the lost-in-the-middle problem by including only content likely to matter for the question.

assessments.prompt: A BPE-style tokenizer's vocabulary is built by starting with individual bytes and repeatedly merging pairs of tokens. Which pairs get merged, and why does that make a random hex string like 'a3f9c2e1' split into far more tokens than a common English phrase of similar length?
options: The tokenizer merges pairs based on a hand-written list of common English morphemes, and hex digits were never added to that list.
Every character is merged with its immediate neighbor exactly once, regardless of frequency, so token count only depends on string length.
Pairs are merged in alphabetical order until the vocabulary reaches its target size, which happens to favor letters over digits.

The most frequently co-occurring adjacent pairs in the training corpus get merged into new tokens; random hex characters rarely repeat the same substring, so no large merged token was ever created for them.
assessments.explanation: BPE vocabularies are learned, not designed: the training process repeatedly finds the most frequent adjacent pair of existing tokens across a large corpus and merges it into one new token, thousands of times over. Common English words and fragments earn big merged tokens because they recur constantly. A random-looking hex string almost never repeats the exact same substring anywhere in the corpus, so the merge process never had a statistical reason to build a larger token for it, leaving it to fall back to small, near-byte-level pieces. The “Pairs are merged in alphabetical order until…”, “The tokenizer merges pairs based…”, and “Every character is merged with its immediate…” options all describe mechanisms BPE does not use -- it is purely frequency-driven, with no alphabetical ordering, no hand-curated morpheme list, and no fixed one-merge-per-character rule.

assessments.prompt: You're assembling a prompt that includes several retrieved facts and a final user question, and only one fact can be flagged as the single most important one. Based on the 'lost in the middle' effect described in this module, where should that critical fact be placed to give the model the best chance of using it correctly?
options: Buried in the exact middle of the context, since models focus attention on the center of long inputs.
Anywhere is equally fine, since a large enough context window guarantees uniform attention across all positions.
Near the very start or the very end of the context, since models empirically attend less reliably to information placed deep in the middle of a long input.
Repeated ten times evenly spaced throughout the context, so at least one occurrence lands in an attended position, whichever part of the input the model attends to.
assessments.explanation: 'Lost in the middle' is a measurable dip in retrieval accuracy for facts placed deep in the middle of a long context, with models making comparatively better use of information near the start and end. The “Anywhere is equally fine, since a large…” option is wrong because a large context window only guarantees a fact fits, not that it's attended to equally well. The “Buried in the exact middle…” option has the effect backwards. The “Repeated ten times evenly spaced throughout…” option adds token cost without addressing the positional effect.

assessments.prompt: A production system needs to answer questions against a knowledge base of 50,000 support articles -- far larger than any model's context window could ever hold at once. Per the strategies discussed in this module, which approach is the best default fit for this specific situation, and why?
options: Chunking and map-reduce: split all 50,000 articles into pieces, summarize every piece for every question, then combine the summaries.
Retrieval: index the articles ahead of time and, for each question, select only the subset of articles actually relevant to it.
Truncation: send as many articles as fit and cut off the rest, since the model can usually infer the missing parts.
Summarization: compress all 50,000 articles into one dense summary once, and reuse that same summary for every future question.
assessments.explanation: Retrieval is the default answer when the overall knowledge base is bigger than the context window, because it selects only the relevant subset per query rather than trying to process everything every time. Truncation risks cutting relevant articles with no way to know what was lost. Running map-reduce summarization across all 50,000 articles for every question is far more wasteful than retrieving the handful of relevant ones. A single static summary of the whole knowledge base would lose the detail needed to answer most questions; summarization suits compressing one oversized input, not standing in for a knowledge base.

concepts.title: Next-Token Prediction: How Generation Actually Works
concepts.description: An LLM writing a paragraph is not planning ahead or outlining the way it appears to: it repeatedly computes a probability distribution over its entire vocabulary and picks one token at a time, each choice conditioned on everything written so far, including its own prior output.
learningObjectives: Describe the autoregressive generation loop: how a model produces a response one token at a time and what makes the loop stop.
Explain what logits and a softmax-derived probability distribution over the vocabulary represent at each generation step.
Explain why the model has no separate planning phase, and what that implies about both its coherence and its failure modes.
Explain why every previously generated token -- including the model's own output -- feeds back in as input to generating the next one.
Predict how changing a single earlier word in a prompt can cascade into a completely different completion.

sections.heading: The Generation Loop: One Token at a Time
sections.body:
Stripped down, text generation from an LLM is a simple loop repeated many times: take the sequence of tokens seen so far (system prompt, conversation history, user message, and any tokens the model has already generated in this response), feed that whole sequence through the model in a single forward pass, get back a probability distribution over every possible next token, select one token from that distribution, append it to the sequence, and repeat -- now with a sequence one token longer than before.

The loop terminates for one of a small number of reasons: the model generates a special end-of-sequence token that it has learned marks 'the response is complete'; the response hits a maximum-length limit you configured; or the generated text matches a stop sequence you specified (a string that, once produced, should end generation immediately, often used to prevent the model from continuing past a clear boundary like the start of a new turn).

Whatever structure, argument, or narrative a long response has was produced by this single-token-at-a-time loop, run enough times in a row. Nothing about the mechanism changes between a one-word answer and a ten-page report. One practical consequence: a response cut off by the maximum-length limit just stops, often mid-sentence, with no sign from the text itself that anything went wrong. Production code should check the finish reason the API returns (named differently by each provider) and treat a length cutoff as a distinct case from a natural stop.

sections.heading: From Logits to Probabilities
sections.body:
At each step of the loop, the model's final layer produces one number, called a **logit**, for every entry in its vocabulary (tens of thousands of numbers or more, one per possible next token), representing (roughly) how strongly the model's learned parameters favor that token as the continuation given everything so far. Those raw logits are not probabilities themselves; a function called **softmax** converts them into a proper probability distribution -- a set of numbers between 0 and 1 that sum to exactly 1 across the whole vocabulary, where a larger logit becomes a larger probability.

The next token is then chosen from that distribution -- either deterministically (always the single highest-probability token, called greedy decoding) or by actually sampling according to the probabilities (which is where temperature and nucleus sampling come in, covered in depth in the next concept). Either way, **no rule-based grammar, lookup table, or symbolic reasoning step chooses the next word**. The choice comes from the learned probability distribution, produced by the same forward pass whether the 'right' next token is obvious ('the' after 'I went to') or uncertain (the next digit of a number the model is fabricating).

sections.heading: No Explicit Plan, Yet Coherent Output
sections.body:
This trips people up because it cuts against how a long, well-structured piece of model output feels to read: there is no separate 'decide the outline, then write the prose' phase in the mechanism above. Every token, including the first word of a ten-paragraph essay, is generated by the same next-token step, conditioned only on the tokens that already exist.

How, then, does the output so often come out globally coherent rather than a word salad? At the scale these models are trained (vast amounts of text, enormous parameter counts), the learned distribution has absorbed the patterns of what coherent, well-structured continuations look like. Predicting what plausibly comes next in text like this appears to require representing something close to topic, tone, and intent internally, as a means of predicting well; nobody designed a planning module.

This shapes how you should think about failure modes. Because there's no separate correction phase, an early token that commits the response to a wrong path (a wrong number, a wrong assumption about what's being asked, an incorrect premise) tends to get reinforced rather than caught, because every subsequent token is generated to be locally coherent with everything already written -- including the model's own mistakes. It's also why asking a model to 'think step by step' helps on harder reasoning problems: it adds no planning module, but it gives the model a place to generate intermediate tokens that it can then condition on when producing the final answer, a better starting point than jumping straight to the answer.

sections.heading: Autoregression: Everything Feeds Back In
sections.body:
The term for this mechanism is **autoregressive generation** -- 'auto' because the model's own previous outputs become part of its future inputs. Every token generated so far in this response, not just your original prompt, conditions the next prediction. That's why a single different word early in a prompt can cascade into a different completion: it shifts the probability distribution at every later step, and each shifted choice becomes part of the context for the step after it, so small differences compound across the length of the response.

One engineering detail you don't need for reasoning about model behavior: because the sequence grows by one token at a time and earlier tokens' internal representations don't change, inference systems use a **KV cache**. They store the intermediate attention results (the keys and values) for tokens already processed and compute only the new work for the newest token, instead of recomputing the whole prefix at every step. It's a pure performance optimization that doesn't change what gets generated, but you'll see the term in inference framework documentation and discussions of generation latency.

examples.title: The Autoregressive Loop, Made Explicit
examples.explanation: This is what happens underneath every call to a hosted chat completion API; the API runs the loop server-side and hides the per-token detail behind one request and response. (It's a sketch: `softmax`, `argmax` and `model` are assumed to exist.) Two lines matter most. `logits = model.forward(tokens)` runs a forward pass over the *entire* sequence so far, including every previously generated token, which is the autoregressive property: the model's own output has become part of its input. (Real inference reuses cached work for the prefix rather than recomputing it; the logic is the same.) And `tokens.append(next_token)` is what lets the loop make progress; forgetting it, or resetting `tokens` each iteration, is an easy bug and the subject of the debugging exercise below. Also note that `model.forward(tokens)` returns logits for every position, and we only use `logits[-1]`, the distribution for the token that comes after everything currently in `tokens`.

examples.title: One Changed Word, a Different Trajectory
examples.code:
prompt_a = "Write one sentence about the weather. It was a sunny day, so"
prompt_b = "Write one sentence about the weather. It was a stormy day, so"

# Both prompts are identical except for one adjective. Because every subsequent
# token is generated conditioned on everything before it, that single word
# shifts the probability distribution at EVERY later generation step, not just
# the very next one -- the two completions typically diverge completely:
#
# prompt_a -> "...everyone decided to go for a walk in the park."
# prompt_b -> "...everyone decided to stay inside and wait it out."
examples.explanation: This is an expected consequence of autoregressive conditioning, not a prompting trick. 'Sunny' versus 'stormy' changes the probability distribution over the next token (what plausibly follows 'so' after each setup), and whichever token gets chosen becomes part of the input for the token after that, and so on. The two completions have no reason to reconverge once they diverge: each new token is generated from whatever the sequence currently contains, with no memory of what the other wording would have implied. The two completions in the comments are illustrative, not captured output. You can see the same effect with any API call: change one word, keep everything else (including the sampling settings) fixed, and compare several runs of each version rather than one. Small, seemingly cosmetic changes to a prompt (word choice, order, an extra clarifying clause) can produce disproportionately different outputs, so evaluate prompt changes empirically instead of assuming they're equivalent because they 'mean the same thing' to a human reader.

examples.title: A Wrong Token Gets Reinforced, Not Caught
examples.code:
prompt = "The Eiffel Tower was completed in the year"

# Suppose the model's next-token step, for whatever reason, assigns the
# highest probability to an incorrect year token, e.g. "1832" instead of
# the correct 1889. Once that token is emitted and appended:
#
# "The Eiffel Tower was completed in the year 1832, during a period of
#  rapid industrial expansion in France..."
#
# Every token after "1832" is generated to be a PLAUSIBLE, FLUENT
# continuation of a sentence that already contains "1832" -- there is no
# step where the model reconsiders whether 1832 was correct in the first place.
examples.explanation: With no planning or self-correction phase, once a token is committed, right or wrong, it becomes an unquestioned part of the context that every later token is conditioned on. The model isn't lying when it builds a fluent, confident-sounding sentence around an incorrect year; it's producing a locally plausible continuation of the text that exists, including its own earlier mistake. This is the generation-mechanism half of why hallucinations read as fluent and self-consistent rather than hedged: nothing in the basic loop makes the model pause and re-examine an earlier claim. The next concept covers the other half: why the wrong token got the highest probability in the first place.

misconceptions.description: The model plans out the overall structure or argument of its response before it starts generating, the way a person might sketch an outline before writing.
misconceptions.clarification: There is no separate planning phase anywhere in the base generation mechanism -- every token, including the first one, is produced by the same next-token-prediction step conditioned only on the text that already exists. Apparent planning is a side effect of the model having learned, from massive amounts of training text, what the early part of a coherent sequence tends to look like; it isn't evidence of a distinct planning module. (Some recent models are trained to produce long reasoning traces before answering, but that is still ordinary token generation.) It's also why prompting a model to write out intermediate reasoning ('think step by step') before its final answer helps on harder problems: it doesn't invoke a hidden planning mechanism, it gives the model explicit tokens to condition later generation on.

misconceptions.description: If a model states something factually wrong partway through a response, it will typically notice and correct itself later in the same response, the way a careful person catches their own mistake mid-sentence.
misconceptions.clarification: The base autoregressive loop has no built-in mechanism that revisits or re-evaluates earlier tokens once they've been generated -- each new token is produced as a plausible continuation of everything already written, including earlier errors, which tends to reinforce a mistake with fluent, consistent-sounding text rather than flag it. (Models can sometimes notice an error mid-response, since text like 'wait, that's wrong' is something they've seen, but you can't rely on it.) Reliable self-correction has to be engineered: a separate verification pass, a tool call that checks a claim, or a prompt that asks the model to critique its own draft as a distinct later step.

exercises.prompt: This simplified generation loop has a bug. What will actually happen when generate() is called -- will it produce a normal-looking multi-token response, get stuck, or something else? Explain why.
exercises.code:
def generate(prompt_tokens, model, max_new_tokens=20, eos_token_id=50256):
    tokens = list(prompt_tokens)
    output = []
    for _ in range(max_new_tokens):
        logits = model.forward(tokens)     # NOTE: always forwards the ORIGINAL tokens
        probs = softmax(logits[-1])
        next_token = argmax(probs)
        if next_token == eos_token_id:
            break
        output.append(next_token)
    return output
hints: Compare this loop to the correct version in the explanation: what happens to the `tokens` list across iterations here versus there?
`model.forward(tokens)` is always called with the same `tokens` list. Does anything in this loop body add the newly generated token back into `tokens`?
If the input to the model never changes between iterations, what would you expect the model's output -- the highest-probability next token -- to do between iterations?
exercises.expectedAnswer: The loop will produce the same token repeated max_new_tokens times (unless that token happens to be the end-of-sequence token, in which case it stops immediately with an empty output), because `tokens` never gets the newly generated token appended to it. Every iteration calls model.forward on the same, unchanging tokens, so the model computes the same probability distribution and greedily picks the same highest-probability token each time.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The bug is that `next_token` is appended to `output` but never appended back to `tokens`, which is what gets fed into `model.forward()` on the next iteration. Since `tokens` is identical on every pass and greedy decoding (`argmax`) is deterministic, the model computes the same logits and picks the same token each time. The loop doesn't crash; it returns a degenerate, repeated-token output. Forgetting to feed the model's own output back in removes the mechanism that lets generation make progress at all.

exercises.prompt: A team's custom local-inference wrapper around an open-weights model produces oddly repetitive output -- long stretches of the same word or phrase repeated over and over. Find the bug in this generation loop and fix it.
hints: Look at which variable gets passed into `model.forward()` each time through the loop, versus which variable accumulates the newly generated tokens.
`tokens` is being correctly appended to at the bottom of the loop -- but is `tokens` the thing actually being fed back into the model on the next pass?
The fix is a one-variable-name change: the model needs to see its own previously generated tokens as part of its input on every subsequent call.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The loop correctly appends each new token to `tokens`, but the call to `model.forward()` was passing `prompt_tokens` -- the original, never-updated prompt -- instead of `tokens`, the list that actually grows as generation proceeds. The model was being asked, over and over, 'what comes right after the original prompt,' with no awareness that it had already generated tokens past that point, so it kept regenerating the most probable token for that position, which produces the repetition described. Swapping `prompt_tokens` for `tokens` in the `forward()` call restores the autoregressive property: each step conditions on the full sequence generated so far.

assessments.prompt: Which of the following best describes how an LLM decides the very next token to output at a given point in generation?
options: It first generates a short outline of the intended response, then fills in each token to match that outline.
It retrieves the most similar sentence from its training data and copies the next word from that sentence.
It looks up the most grammatically correct next word using a rule-based grammar engine trained alongside the model.
It computes a probability distribution over its entire vocabulary, conditioned on all tokens generated so far (prompt plus its own prior output), and selects a token from that distribution.
assessments.explanation: A forward pass produces one logit per vocabulary entry, softmax converts those into a probability distribution, and a token is selected from it -- with the entire process conditioned on every token that already exists in the sequence, including tokens the model itself generated earlier in the same response. The “It looks up the most grammatically correct…” option is wrong because no separate symbolic grammar engine is involved; grammatical patterns are represented implicitly in the learned distribution. The “It retrieves the most similar sentence…” option is wrong because the model doesn't look up stored training sentences at generation time; it generates from learned parameters, not a searchable copy of its training data. The “It first generates a short outline…” option is wrong because the base mechanism has no distinct outlining phase; apparent structure emerges from token-by-token prediction, unless an intermediate-reasoning step is added through prompting.

assessments.prompt: Explain, strictly in terms of the autoregressive next-token-prediction mechanism, why explicitly asking a model to 'think step by step' before giving its final answer often improves accuracy on multi-step reasoning problems.
assessments.modelAnswer: Every token a model generates is conditioned on everything already in the sequence: the prompt plus every token generated so far in this response. The model has little room to 'work something out' beyond what its fixed number of layers can compute in one forward pass, so extended reasoning has to exist as generated tokens. If you demand only a final answer to a multi-step question, the model has to produce it as essentially the very next token(s), conditioned on nothing but the question, with no intermediate scratch space. Asking the model to 'think step by step' changes what gets generated before the final answer: the model produces intermediate tokens (restating the problem, working through sub-steps, computing intermediate quantities), and every one of them becomes context that the final-answer tokens are conditioned on. You're not invoking a hidden reasoning module; you're using the same next-token mechanism to generate a scratchpad, then letting the model condition its answer on it instead of jumping from question to answer with nothing in between. Each step is a smaller, more locally predictable leap when the relevant earlier work is already on the page, so the final answer tends to be more accurate than one produced by solving the whole multi-step problem in a single leap.

assessments.prompt: At each step of the generation loop, what does the model's final layer compute before a next token is chosen?
options: A ranked shortlist of the five most likely next words, computed by comparing against stored training sentences, with everything outside it set to zero.
One logit per vocabulary entry, which softmax then converts into a probability distribution over the entire vocabulary that sums to 1.
A binary flag for every vocabulary entry indicating whether that token is grammatically valid at this position.
A single probability value representing how confident the model is in its overall response so far.
assessments.explanation: The model produces one logit per vocabulary entry (tens of thousands of numbers or more), and softmax converts them into a probability distribution over the whole vocabulary that sums to 1. The “A single probability value representing how confident…” option is wrong because no single 'overall confidence' scalar is computed at each step, only a distribution over the next token. The “A ranked shortlist of the five most…” option is wrong because generation doesn't compare against stored training sentences at inference time. The “A binary flag for every vocabulary entry…” option is wrong because there's no separate grammar-validity check; grammaticality is reflected in the learned logit values, not a pass/fail flag.

assessments.prompt: Which of the following is NOT one of the ways the basic autoregressive generation loop actually terminates, according to this module?
options: The generated text matches a configured stop sequence.
The response reaches a configured maximum-length limit.
The model internally recognizes it has 'sufficiently answered' the question and raises a distinct completion signal separate from any generated token.
The model generates a special end-of-sequence token it has learned marks the response as complete.
assessments.explanation: The loop has three termination conditions: an end-of-sequence token, a max-length limit, and a matched stop sequence. Each is either a token the model generates or configuration you set. The correct answer describes a mechanism that doesn't exist in the base loop: no separate internal 'I'm done' signal exists apart from the tokens produced.

assessments.prompt: Two prompts are identical except that one early word differs ('sunny' vs. 'stormy'), yet their multi-sentence completions end up completely different, not just different in that one spot. What mechanism explains why the difference cascades rather than staying local?
options: Each generated token is conditioned on every token that precedes it.
The tokenizer assigns a different total token budget depending on which adjective is used, changing how much room is left for the response.
Different adjectives route the prompt to different hard-coded response templates stored in the model's weights.
The model re-plans and rewrites the entire response from scratch whenever any single input word changes.
assessments.explanation: Autoregressive generation conditions every new token on the entire sequence so far, including tokens the model itself already generated in this response. A different early word shifts the probability distribution at the next step; whichever token gets picked then becomes part of the context for the step after that, so a small initial difference compounds. There's no re-planning phase (“The model re-plans and rewrites the entire…”), no template-routing mechanism (“Different adjectives route the prompt to different…”), and adjective choice doesn't change the token budget in the way the “The tokenizer assigns a different total token…” option describes.

concepts.title: Sampling, Temperature, and Why Models Hallucinate
concepts.description: Temperature and sampling strategy control how a model turns its next-token probability distribution into a chosen token, and that same probabilistic mechanism, not a database lookup or a fact-checking step, is the root cause of hallucination, which is why sampling-parameter tuning alone cannot eliminate it.
learningObjectives: Explain what the temperature parameter does mathematically to a next-token probability distribution, and predict its qualitative effect at low, moderate, and high settings.
Compare greedy decoding, temperature sampling, and top-p (nucleus) sampling, and choose an appropriate strategy for a given use case.
Explain why hallucination is an expected consequence of the training objective and generation mechanism rather than a rare software defect.
Explain why temperature 0 (greedy decoding) reduces output variance but does not reduce hallucination rate.
Identify concrete hallucination mitigation strategies and articulate why each one reduces, but cannot fully eliminate, the underlying risk.

sections.heading: What Temperature Does to the Distribution
sections.body:
Recall from the previous concept that the model's final layer produces one logit per vocabulary token, and softmax converts those logits into a probability distribution. **Temperature** is a single number that gets applied just before that softmax step: every logit is divided by the temperature value before the softmax conversion happens.

The effect of that division isn't intuitive at first. Dividing by a temperature **less than 1** makes the differences between logits larger, which softmax converts into a *more sharply peaked* distribution: the already-most-probable tokens become even more dominant, and choices become more consistent across repeated calls. Dividing by a temperature **greater than 1** does the opposite: it shrinks the differences between logits and flattens the distribution, giving moderately probable tokens a better chance of being selected, which produces more varied, sometimes more creative, and also more erratic output. **Temperature 0** is a special-cased limit rather than a literal division (dividing by zero is undefined): APIs generally treat it as 'skip sampling, always pick the highest-probability token,' which is greedy decoding. (Some newer models, such as reasoning models, don't let you set temperature at all, and the allowed range differs by provider; check your provider's docs.)

```python
response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="gpt-4.1",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "List three uses for a paperclip."}],
    temperature=0.2,   # sharply peaked: consistent, conservative, low variety across calls
)
```

A useful mental model: temperature doesn't change which token the model ranks as most probable; it changes how strictly selection sticks to that ranking versus exploring less-probable alternatives.

sections.heading: Beyond Temperature: Top-k and Top-p (Nucleus) Sampling
sections.body:
Temperature reshapes the whole distribution but doesn't remove the long tail of implausible tokens: even a token with a tiny probability keeps a nonzero chance of being selected, and a high temperature raises it. Two additional techniques address this by restricting *which* tokens are eligible for selection.

**Top-k sampling** restricts the candidate pool to only the k highest-probability tokens (say, the top 40), then samples from just that restricted pool. This is simple but awkward: a fixed k is sometimes too restrictive (when the distribution is flat and spread across many reasonable options) and sometimes too permissive (when the distribution is sharp, only two or three tokens are plausible, and k=40 still lets bad options into the pool).

**Top-p sampling** (also called **nucleus sampling**) fixes that problem by making the pool size adaptive: instead of a fixed count, it includes the smallest set of highest-probability tokens whose cumulative probability reaches some threshold p (commonly around 0.9 or 0.95). When the model is very confident and the distribution is sharply peaked, the nucleus might contain only two or three tokens; when the model is uncertain and the distribution is spread out, the nucleus grows to include more candidates. This adaptivity is why top-p is often preferred over a fixed top-k. Many APIs expose both temperature and top_p, and they interact (implementations differ on the order in which they're applied), so the usual advice, which several providers' docs give, is to adjust one and leave the other at its default.

sections.heading: Hallucination Is the Mechanism Working as Designed
sections.body:
The key reframing about hallucination: the model was trained to predict plausible, fluent continuations of text, not to assert only verified facts, and no module in the architecture checks a generated claim against ground truth before it's emitted. Nothing in the generation step marks a token as 'verified true' as opposed to 'the most locally plausible continuation.' (Token probabilities do carry some information about confidence, and researchers use them for calibration, but they're a noisy guide and the fluent text doesn't reflect them.) A correct fact and a fabricated one come out of the same probability distribution, computed by the same mechanism. In practice the risk concentrates in specific places: obscure people, products or APIs the model saw rarely; exact figures, dates and quotations; and anything that looks like a reference, such as a citation, a URL or a function name. Those are the outputs worth verifying first.

That's why hallucinated content so often reads as fluent, confident, and well structured as correct content: nothing in generation marks a fabrication differently from a verified statement, because the training objective rewarded fluency and plausibility, not calibrated truthfulness. A model that learned a fact well (it appeared frequently, consistently, and unambiguously in training data) will usually reproduce it reliably, because that is the highest-probability continuation. A model asked about something rare, ambiguous, contradictory across sources, or outside its training will still produce *a* highest-probability continuation, fluent and formatted like a correct answer, because producing something plausible-sounding is what the mechanism does every time it's asked for a next token.

sections.heading: Why Temperature 0 Doesn't Fix It
sections.body:
A common intuition is that setting temperature to 0 makes the model 'more careful' or 'more truthful' because it removes randomness. What temperature 0 removes is *sampling variance*: the model picks the highest-probability token at every step, every time, rather than occasionally sampling a different one. It does **not** change which token the model considers most probable.

If the model's learned distribution happens to assign the highest probability to an incorrect fact -- a plausible-sounding but wrong function signature, a fabricated citation, an incorrect date -- greedy decoding will produce that same wrong answer every time you ask. Temperature 0 gives up the chance of an occasionally different (and possibly correct) sampled alternative in exchange for determinism around the model's single most-probable guess, right or wrong. Raising temperature doesn't reliably fix hallucination either: it samples more from the tail, which can introduce a new fabrication as easily as surface a better answer. No dial trades cleanly between 'more deterministic' and 'more truthful'; determinism and correctness are different, largely unrelated axes.

sections.heading: Mitigations and Their Limits
sections.body: None of these make hallucination impossible, because none change the underlying probabilistic generation mechanism, but each reduces its likelihood or its blast radius, which is why real systems combine several. **Grounding via retrieval** (the next module) narrows the space of plausible continuations by putting relevant, verified text in the context, so the highest-probability continuation is far more likely to match that material; in practice it is among the most effective levers available. **Lowering temperature** reduces run-to-run variance, which helps consistency and reproducibility but, as covered above, doesn't by itself improve correctness. **Asking for citations or sources** can help, but only if you verify that the cited source exists and says what's claimed; a model can hallucinate a fake citation with the same fluent confidence as any other claim. **Verification passes** (asking the model to quote the exact span of a source it relies on, or running a second, independent pass that checks a claim against retrieved evidence) add cost and latency but catch cases the first pass got wrong. Underneath all of this: as long as correct and incorrect statements come out of the same probabilistic process, no purely generative technique reduces the risk to zero. Where being wrong is costly, external verification or grounding is a requirement.

examples.title: The Same Prompt at Three Temperatures
examples.code:
# fragment: assumes an initialised OpenAI-style `client`
prompt = "Suggest a name for a new coffee shop."

for temp in [0.0, 0.7, 1.3]:
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="gpt-4.1",
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
        temperature=temp,
    )
    print(temp, "->", response.choices[0].message.content)

# temp=0.0 -> "The Daily Grind"          (same answer basically every run)
# temp=0.7 -> "Brew & Co."                (varies moderately across runs)
# temp=1.3 -> "Percolate Dreams Cafe"     (more varied, occasionally odd, across runs)
examples.explanation: At temperature 0, selection is greedy: run this many times and you get the same or nearly the same answer, because no sampling randomness is left. (The names in the comments are illustrative.) At a moderate temperature like 0.7, the distribution still favors likely candidates but leaves enough probability on other reasonable options that repeated calls explore different, still-sensible names. At 1.3, the distribution is flat enough that unusual tokens get selected more often, which can read as 'creative' but can drift into names that are incoherent or off-brief; flattening the distribution surfaces bad unlikely options as readily as good ones. That's why creative-writing or brainstorming features tend to use higher temperatures, while factual Q&A, classification, or code generation tend to use low or zero temperature, not because low temperature makes answers more correct but because it makes them consistent, which matters when variety isn't the goal.

examples.title: Greedy Decoding Still Hallucinates, Consistently
examples.code:
# fragment: assumes an initialised OpenAI-style `client`
prompt = "What year was the Python programming language first released, and by whom?"

for _ in range(3):
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="some-model",
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
        temperature=0.0,
    )
    print(response.choices[0].message.content)

# Suppose, hypothetically, a weaker or older model's most-probable answer here
# were subtly wrong -- e.g. citing the wrong year or the wrong original author.
# At temperature 0.0, all three calls would return that SAME wrong answer,
# with identical confident phrasing every single time.
examples.explanation: This example is about the *shape* of the failure, not any real model's accuracy on this fact (Python was first released in 1991 by Guido van Rossum; the hypothetical wrong answer is only there to show the mechanism). If a model's distribution puts the highest probability on an incorrect answer, for any reason, including ambiguous or sparse training signal, temperature 0 gives it no chance to land on a different, possibly correct, answer; it reproduces that output every time. So 'the model gave me the same wrong answer three times in a row' is not corroboration: consistency at temperature 0 reflects the determinism of greedy decoding, not independent confirmation. To verify a factual claim, check it against a source instead of asking the same deterministic model again.

examples.title: Top-p Adapting to How Peaked the Distribution Is
examples.code:
# fragment: assumes an initialised OpenAI-style `client`
# Step where the next token is nearly certain -- e.g. completing "Thank you very"
# The distribution might be: {"much": 0.94, "kindly": 0.03, ...tiny tail...}
# With top_p=0.9, the nucleus contains essentially just "much" -- barely any
# alternative gets included, because one token alone already exceeds 0.9.

# Step where many continuations are genuinely reasonable -- e.g. completing
# "My favorite hobby is"
# The distribution might be spread across many options: {"reading": 0.12,
# "hiking": 0.10, "cooking": 0.09, "painting": 0.07, ...many more...}
# With the same top_p=0.9, the nucleus now has to include many more tokens
# before their cumulative probability crosses 0.9.

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="gpt-4.1",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "My favorite hobby is"}],
    top_p=0.9,
    temperature=0.8,
)
examples.explanation: The advantage of top-p over a fixed top-k shows in this contrast: the same top_p=0.9 gives a tiny, almost-certain nucleus at the first (near-deterministic) step and a much larger nucleus at the second (open-ended) step, because the boundary is set by cumulative probability, not a fixed count. (The probabilities in the comments are made up for illustration.) A fixed top-k=40 would consider 40 candidates at the first step too, though only one or two are reasonable, leaving the door open to a clearly wrong completion of 'Thank you very' that a human would never produce. Top-p tracks the model's confidence at each step instead of applying one fixed rule regardless of how sharp or flat the distribution is.

misconceptions.description: Setting temperature to 0 makes the model 'more careful,' 'more honest,' or otherwise more likely to be factually correct.
misconceptions.clarification: Temperature 0 only removes sampling randomness: the model always picks the highest-probability token (greedy decoding) instead of sometimes sampling a different one. It doesn't change which token the model's parameters consider most probable. If that top answer is wrong, temperature 0 reproduces the same wrong answer every time instead of occasionally landing on a different, possibly correct, one. Determinism and correctness are largely independent; temperature controls the former, not the latter.

misconceptions.description: When a model states something false, it's because it 'doesn't know' the answer, and if it truly didn't know, it would say so or express uncertainty, the way a person would.
misconceptions.clarification: The model has no separate fact-checking step at generation time that distinguishes 'a fact I've reliably learned' from 'the most plausible-sounding continuation, true or not'; both come from the same probability distribution. Hedging is not an automatic behavior that kicks in when the model 'doesn't know' something; it appears only when training or prompting conditions the model to hedge in that situation (models can be trained to abstain more often, but it's imperfect). Fluent, confident phrasing is therefore not evidence that a claim is correct.

exercises.prompt: The same prompt is sent to a chat completion API twice at temperature=0.0, and separately, twice at temperature=1.2. Predict whether each pair of calls is likely to return identical text, and explain the difference between the two pairs.
exercises.code:
# fragment: assumes an initialised OpenAI-style `client`
for _ in range(2):
    r = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="gpt-4.1",
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Name a color."}],
        temperature=0.0,
    )
    print("temp=0.0:", r.choices[0].message.content)

for _ in range(2):
    r = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="gpt-4.1",
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Name a color."}],
        temperature=1.2,
    )
    print("temp=1.2:", r.choices[0].message.content)
hints: Most APIs treat temperature 0 as a special case. What sampling behavior does it collapse to?
At a high temperature, the distribution over next tokens is flattened, giving lower-probability tokens a real chance of being selected. Does that make repeated calls more or less likely to agree?

Note: some providers' infrastructure introduces small amounts of nondeterminism even at temperature 0 (for performance reasons), so 'identical' in practice often means 'nearly always identical.' The contrast between the two settings should still hold.
exercises.expectedAnswer: The two temperature=0.0 calls are very likely to return the same color, because temperature 0 collapses to greedy decoding, always selecting the highest-probability token. The two temperature=1.2 calls are more likely to differ, because the flattened distribution gives several plausible colors a real chance of being sampled on each independent call (they can still agree by chance).
exercises.solutionExplanation: At temperature 0.0, the model (via the greedy shortcut most APIs implement) returns the most probable token at each step; with no randomness in selection, repeated identical calls should return the same or nearly the same output. At temperature 1.2, the distribution is flattened, spreading meaningful probability across several plausible colors, so each call is an independent random draw from that broader set and two draws landing on the same color is far less certain. Temperature governs how much randomness enters selection, not what the model ranks as most probable, which is why it affects consistency but not correctness.

exercises.prompt: A customer-support bot is fabricating policy details (wrong refund windows, invented exceptions) that don't match the company's policy. The team's first fix attempt was to set temperature to 0, reasoning that this would make the bot 'stick to the facts.' The hallucinations continued at the same rate. Diagnose why this fix didn't work, and propose one that actually addresses the root cause.
exercises.code:
# fragment: assumes an initialised OpenAI-style `client`
response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="gpt-4.1",
    messages=[
        {"role": "system", "content": "You are a helpful customer support assistant. Answer accurately."},
        {"role": "user", "content": user_question},
    ],
    temperature=0.0,   # the team's attempted fix
)
hints: What does temperature control: the model's underlying probabilities, or only how deterministically it acts on them?
The system message says 'answer accurately,' but does the model have access to the company's current policy anywhere in this request?
Without the real policy text present in the context somewhere, what is the model's 'most probable continuation' actually based on?
exercises.solutionCode:
# fragment: assumes an initialised OpenAI-style `client`
policy_chunks = retrieve_relevant_policy(user_question)   # e.g. from a vector index of the real policy docs
context_text = "\n\n".join(policy_chunks)

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="gpt-4.1",
    messages=[
        {"role": "system", "content": (
            "You are a customer support assistant. Answer ONLY using the policy "
            "excerpts provided below. If the answer isn't contained in the excerpts, "
            "say you don't know and offer to escalate to a human.\n\n"
            f"Policy excerpts:\n{context_text}"
        )},
        {"role": "user", "content": user_question},
    ],
    temperature=0.0,
)
exercises.solutionExplanation: Temperature only controls how deterministically the model acts on its probability distribution; it doesn't change what the distribution contains, and the original request never gave the model the policy text, just an instruction to 'answer accurately' with nothing to be accurate *from*. With no grounding text, the model's highest-probability continuation is generic, plausible-sounding policy language from its training data, whatever the temperature. The fix is grounding: retrieve the current policy text relevant to the question and put it in the prompt, with an instruction to answer only from that text (and say so, rather than guess, if the answer isn't there). This doesn't make hallucination impossible, but it gives the model true text to condition on, which is what reduces fabrication.

assessments.prompt: Setting a model's temperature parameter to 0 primarily has which effect?
options: It reduces the model's vocabulary to only the most common, 'safe' words.
It makes the model check its answer against external sources before responding.
It forces the model to always select the single highest-probability token at each step (greedy decoding), removing sampling randomness but not changing which token is most probable.
It guarantees the model will express uncertainty whenever it is unsure of an answer.
assessments.explanation: Temperature 0 is the special-cased limit where sampling is replaced by always picking the argmax (highest-probability) token, making output deterministic across identical calls, but it leaves the underlying probabilities unchanged, so an incorrect top answer stays incorrect and is reproduced consistently. The “It makes the model check its answer…” option describes something no temperature setting provides; verification needs a separate step like retrieval or a check pass. The “It reduces the model's vocabulary to only…” option is wrong because temperature reshapes the probability distribution over the existing vocabulary; it doesn't remove words from it. The “It guarantees the model will express uncertainty…” option is wrong because expressing uncertainty isn't triggered by any sampling setting; it happens only if the model has learned to produce hedging language in that situation.

assessments.prompt: A colleague argues: 'if the model can hallucinate a wrong fact with the exact same fluent, confident tone as a correct one, how are users supposed to trust anything it says?' Explain why this happens in terms of the generation mechanism, and what it implies for how you should design a product that surfaces LLM output directly to end users.
assessments.modelAnswer: Fluency and factual correctness are not linked in the generation mechanism: every token, whether it states a verified fact or a fabricated one, is produced by the same next-token process, drawing from a distribution shaped by what's statistically plausible given the training data and context, with no check against ground truth. Nothing makes correct statements sound different from incorrect ones; a hallucinated claim gets the same grammar, assertive phrasing, and tone as a true one. For product design, that means you can't use the model's tone as a reliability signal, and you should assume every factual output needs grounding, verification, or an acknowledgment of uncertainty to the user. In practice that points to retrieval-augmented generation for anything factual (so claims are traceable to a source you can show), citations that a human or a separate process verifies, UI that makes clear when content is AI-generated and unverified, and reserving ungrounded generation for low-stakes uses (brainstorming, creative drafts) where an occasional plausible-but-wrong output does no harm. Trustworthiness has to be engineered around the generation mechanism; you can't read it off the model's tone.

assessments.prompt: How does top-p (nucleus) sampling decide which tokens are eligible for selection, and how does that differ from top-k sampling?
options: Top-p selects tokens alphabetically from among the top-k highest-probability candidates.

Top-p includes the smallest set of highest-probability tokens whose cumulative probability exceeds a threshold, so the pool size adapts to how peaked or flat the distribution is at each step; top-k always uses a fixed candidate count regardless of the distribution's shape.
Top-p is only applied when temperature is set to 0, while top-k is only applied at nonzero temperature.
Top-p and top-k are two names for the exact same mechanism, differing only in which APIs expose which name.
assessments.explanation: Top-p's pool boundary is set by cumulative probability crossing a threshold p, so a sharply peaked distribution yields a tiny nucleus and a flat one a larger nucleus; it adapts per step. Top-k always considers k candidates however peaked or flat the distribution is, which is the limitation top-p was designed to fix. The “Top-p and top-k are two names…”, “Top-p selects tokens alphabetically from among…”, and “Top-p is only applied when temperature…” options all misstate the mechanisms: they are distinct techniques, neither is alphabetical, and neither is gated on a specific temperature value.

assessments.prompt: Which statement about hallucination mitigation strategies best matches this module's discussion of their real limits?
options: Asking the model to provide citations is sufficient on its own, since a model that fabricates facts will not also fabricate a citation.
Grounding via retrieval eliminates hallucination entirely, since a grounded model can only ever repeat the retrieved text verbatim.
Setting temperature to 0 is the most effective mitigation, since it removes the sampling randomness that causes hallucination.
Retrieval meaningfully reduces hallucination risk by narrowing the space of plausible continuations.
assessments.explanation: Grounding via retrieval is among the most effective levers but does not make hallucination impossible, because it doesn't change the underlying probabilistic generation mechanism; external verification remains necessary wherever being wrong is costly. The “Grounding via retrieval eliminates hallucination entirely, since…” option overstates retrieval's guarantee. The “Asking the model to provide citations…” option is contradicted by the fact that a model can hallucinate a fake citation as fluently as any other claim. The “Setting temperature to 0 is the most…” option is wrong because temperature only affects sampling variance, not which answer the model considers most probable, so it doesn't reduce hallucination rate.

assessments.prompt: Why do hallucinated statements typically come out just as fluent and confident-sounding as accurate ones, rather than hedged or tentative?
options: Both correct and fabricated tokens are produced by the identical next-token-prediction mechanism optimizing for locally plausible continuation, and there is no internal signal at generation time distinguishing a verified fact from a plausible-sounding fabrication.
Hedging phrases are removed from the vocabulary by default and must be manually re-enabled through a configuration flag.
A dedicated confidence-estimation module miscalibrates specifically on false statements, making them sound artificially confident.
Models are explicitly trained with a reward signal that punishes hedging language regardless of correctness.
assessments.explanation: Hallucination is the generation mechanism working as designed, not a distinct malfunction: every token, true or fabricated, is produced by the same distribution optimizing for plausible continuation, with no 'this is verified' marker in the process. Hedging appears only when training data or prompting conditions the model to produce it in that situation; it isn't a default reaction to low confidence. The “A dedicated confidence-estimation module miscalibrates specifically…”, “Models are explicitly trained with a reward…”, and “Hedging phrases are removed from the vocabulary…” options each invent a mechanism (a confidence estimator, an anti-hedging reward, a disabled vocabulary subset) that isn't how these models work.
